blocks.text: Isaiah’s warning about seeking Egypt’s horses, chariots, and horsemen can be read against a disputed interpretation of Assyrian-era politics: reliance on foreign coalitions and military strength is treated as a religious as well as a political issue. The contrast between Egypt as human and its horses as flesh, and the Holy One of Israel, presses the chapter’s question of where Judah places its trust.

A debated observation about the book surrounding this chapter concerns the Great Isaiah Scroll: it preserves almost the entire sixty-six-chapter book and broadly aligns with the Masoretic tradition, while also containing thousands of spelling and substantive differences. Other Isaiah manuscripts and interpretive writings from Qumran likewise show that Isaiah was actively copied and interpreted.
